fixes.explanation: Right on the money, baker. God says Jerusalem is the daughter of her mother, who "…despised her husband and children." (Ezekiel 16:45) That's the family resemblance the proverb points to. I think this one is heavy, because it's about turning away from the people closest to you.

Yes, baker! God says, "Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) Samaria is the older sister here, and she had her daughters with her. Jerusalem's family is bigger than just the one sister.

God doesn't name Damascus here, friend. He says Jerusalem's older sister "…was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) It's a fair guess when you're picturing a northern neighbor. The verse just gives a different name.

The verse names someone else, friend: "Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) Samaria is the one God puts in the family. Tyre isn't in this lineup at all.

Bethel isn't the sister here, friend. God says, "…your younger sister was Sodom, who lived with her daughters to your south." (Ezekiel 16:46) Sodom is the name He gives. Bethel doesn't show up in this verse.

Babylon isn't the sister here, friend. In this verse God names the younger sister as Sodom, who "…lived with her daughters to your south." (Ezekiel 16:46) Babylon isn't part of this family. The sisters are Samaria and Sodom.

You got it, baker. God says she walked in their ways and practiced their abominations, "…but soon you were more depraved than they were." (Ezekiel 16:47) She didn't just follow her sisters. She went further than they did. I think this verse is a heavy one.

That's not what God says, friend. Jerusalem "…walked in their ways and practiced their abominations…" and "…soon you were more depraved than they were." (Ezekiel 16:47) The verse doesn't say she warned them. It says she walked in their ways and then went further.

Proud isn't the word here, friend. God says, "…you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them." (Ezekiel 16:54) So the feeling the verse names is shame. It doesn't name pride.

Right, baker. God asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) That was before her own wickedness was uncovered. I think this one stings a little.

That's not what God says, friend. He asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) Scorn is the word. Rescue isn't what the verse describes.

A visit sounds nice, but that's not the picture. God asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) So she looked down on Sodom. Scorn is the word the verse uses.

True, baker. God says, "I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:61) That's in the same verse where Jerusalem remembers her ways and is ashamed when she receives her older and younger sisters. The family gets bigger.

Her sisters aren't what she'll know, friend. God says, "…you will know that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 16:62) That's what she'll know when He establishes His covenant. The verse puts the focus on who He is.
